A '''wildlife population''' or '''species population''' is the concept of "[[Population (biology)|population]]" applied to any species other than humans. Understanding a wildlife population requires a [[census]] of the species, and the technique for accomplishing that vary depending on the species and circumstance.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Marshall |first1=Howard Wight |title=Field and Laboratory Technic in Wildlife Management |date=1939 |publisher=University of Michigan Press |location=Ann Arbor |pages=23-30 |URL=https://www.fulcrum.org/epubs/9306t2325?locale=en#page=29 |chapter=Census Methods}}</ref> Characteristics which define a wildlife population include [[population density]], [[birth rate]], [[mortality rate]], [[age distribution]], [[biotic potential]], [[biological dispersal]], and [[growth form]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Odum |first1=Eugene |author1-link=Eugene Odum |title=Fundamentals of Ecology |date=1953 |publisher=[[W. B. Saunders Company]] |location=Athens, Georgia |page=91 |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofec00odum1/page/90/mode/2up |chapter=Principles and Concepts Pertaining to Organization at the Species Population Level}}</ref>

Methods for measuring wildlife populations include [[mark and recapture]], [[distance sampling]], and examining a [[harvest]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buckland |first1=S. T. |last2=Goudie |first2=I. B. J. |last3=Borchers |first3=D. L. |title=Wildlife Population Assessment: Past Developments and Future Directions |journal=Biometrics |date=March 2000 |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1111/j.0006-341X.2000.00001.x}}</ref> Biologists who survey wildlife populations often work in a business context where they balance maintaining quality data, but complete the survey quickly, and work at low cost.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Witmer |first1=Gary W. |title=Wildlife population monitoring: some practical considerations |journal=Wildlife Research |date=23 June 2005 |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=259–263 |doi=10.1071/WR04003}}</ref> Economic reasons for doing wildlife surveys can include harvesting wildlife, controlling disease, or negotiating conflicts between multiple business interests who claim control of a resource.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gren |first1=Ing-Marie |last2=Häggmark-Svensson |first2=Tobias |last3=Elofsson |first3=Katarina |last4=Engelmann |first4=Marc |title=Economics of wildlife management—an overview |journal=European Journal of Wildlife Research |date=April 2018 |volume=64 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/s10344-018-1180-3|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Motivations for studying wildlife populations include [[wildlife conservation]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mills |first1=L. Scott |last2=Whiteley |first2=Andrew R. |last3=Tourani |first3=Mahdieh |title=Conservation of wildlife populations: applications of ecological, evolutionary, and genetic concepts |date=2025 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=New York |isbn=978-0192898166 |edition=3}}</ref> and [[wildlife management]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Frankham |first1=Richard |title=Genetic Management of Fragmented Animal and Plant Populations |date=2017 |publisher=Oxford University Press USA - OSO |location=Oxford |isbn=9780191086069}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Krausman |editor1-first=Paul R. |editor2-last=Cain III |editor2-first=James W. |title=Wildlife management and conservation: contemporary principles and practices |date=2022 |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |location=Baltimore |isbn=978-1421443966 |edition=Second}}</ref>

Wildlife populations are declining globally at fast rates. The [[Living Planet Index]] reported that from 1970-2020, the global populations in [[freshwater ecosystem]]s have decreased by 85%, [[Terrestrial animal]]s by 69%, and [[marine life]] by 56%.<ref name="WWF 2024">{{cite book |author1=WWF |author1-link=World Wide Fund for Nature |title=2024 Living Planet Report - A System in Peril |date=October 10, 2024 |location=[[Gland, Switzerland]] |page=7 |url=https://www.worldwildlife.org/publications/2024-living-planet-report/}}</ref> Counting the number of individuals in a population is key to predicting and identifying [[ecosystem collapse]] when populations of wildlife will go extinct.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cerini |first1=Francesco |last2=Childs |first2=Dylan Z. |last3=Clements |first3=Christopher F. |title=A predictive timeline of wildlife population collapse |journal=Nature Ecology & Evolution |date=26 January 2023 |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=320–331 |doi=10.1038/s41559-023-01985-2|hdl=1983/83a15c48-7f9b-4a31-9e57-459b44a21927 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ripple |first1=William J. |last2=Newsome |first2=Thomas M. |last3=Wolf |first3=Christopher |last4=Dirzo |first4=Rodolfo |last5=Everatt |first5=Kristoffer T. |last6=Galetti |first6=Mauro |last7=Hayward |first7=Matt W. |last8=Kerley |first8=Graham I. H. |last9=Levi |first9=Taal |last10=Lindsey |first10=Peter A. |last11=Macdonald |first11=David W. |last12=Malhi |first12=Yadvinder |last13=Painter |first13=Luke E. |last14=Sandom |first14=Christopher J. |last15=Terborgh |first15=John |last16=Van Valkenburgh |first16=Blaire |title=Collapse of the world’s largest herbivores |journal=Science Advances |date=May 2015 |volume=1 |issue=4 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.1400103|hdl=11449/177864 |hdl-access=free |pmc=4640652 }}</ref> [[Population viability analysis]] is a method for determining if a population will go extinct in given circumstances.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lacy |first1=Robert C. |title=Lessons from 30 years of population viability analysis of wildlife populations |journal=Zoo Biology |date=January 2019 |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=67–77 |doi=10.1002/zoo.21468}}</ref>
